title: Grace Hopper's A-0 helped replace numeric instructions with words
body: In 1952 Grace Hopper completed A-0, a system that could assemble previously prepared routines into a program. It let the operator specify routines using a more human-readable notation than the computer's raw instructions.
takeaway: Reusing prepared pieces of code means each new program need not start from the machine's smallest operations.
source: Computer History Museum, Timeline of Computer History (1952)
visual: a programmer's hand beside an early mainframe tape drive

title: An early trackball used a Canadian bowling ball
body: Around 1952, Canada's DATAR naval defence system used a ball from five-pin bowling as a controller for radar displays. The operator rolled the ball in place to guide the pointer.
takeaway: A trackball gives the operator two dimensions of control while the base stays put, useful at a crowded console.
visual: a smooth bowling ball cradled in a steel console beside the glow of a round radar display
